<reason>Both sides built coherent cases, but CON identified and relentlessly exploited the structural weak point in PRO's position: PRO's own attempt to reconcile a "ban" with permitting systems like Aegis/Patriot (via a target-and-context carve-out in A4.1) let CON argue convincingly that PRO's workable version of the resolution collapses into the very "calibrated regulation" CON proposed from the opening. CON's pressure question on Aegis was answered by PRO in a way that CON then turned into the centerpiece of Rebuttal 2 and Closing, framing a clean dichotomy PRO never fully dismantled ("either the ban catches Aegis and loses its own example, or it doesn't and is indistinguishable from regulation"). PRO's closing gestured at a rebuttal (a ban permits one function and forbids another categorically, regardless of testing) but did not develop this distinction sharply enough to neutralize CON's framing. CON also landed solid counters on proliferation (China/Russia as leading developers, not laggards waiting on export licenses) that PRO answered with a somewhat generic assertion about "concentrated testing ranges." PRO's moral/accountability arguments remained live and were not fully destroyed, keeping this competitive, but CON's cleaner, more strategically focused rebuttal sequence and superior closing framing made the debate easier to decide in CON's favor.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's use of PRO's own Pressure-Question answer (A4.1's "target and context" carve-out permitting Aegis-like interception) as proof that PRO's ban is indistinguishable from CON's proposed regulation, driven home in Rebuttal 2 and restated as a decisive dichotomy in Closing, was the most damaging and unanswered exchange of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
